claim: RXRA regulates transcription as part of a heterodimer with 14 other nuclear receptors, including the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs).
source: RXRA regulates transcription as part of a heterodimer with 14 other nuclear receptors, including the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about RXRA function and its heterodimerization partners.

claim: RXRA hot-spot mutation (S427F/Y) is found in 5-8% of bladder cancer cases.
source: Exome analysis of bladder cancer samples across three independent cohorts identified mutations at RXRA S427 in 5–8% of cases, always leading to an amino acid substitution with an aromatic amino acid, phenylalanine (~5%) or tyrosine (~1%) (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Guo et al., 2013; Van Allen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three independent cohort studies analyzing bladder cancer exomes.

claim: RXRA S427 mutations always lead to substitution with an aromatic amino acid (phenylalanine or tyrosine).
source: Exome analysis of bladder cancer samples across three independent cohorts identified mutations at RXRA S427 in 5–8% of cases, always leading to an amino acid substitution with an aromatic amino acid, phenylalanine (~5%) or tyrosine (~1%) (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Guo et al., 2013; Van Allen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three independent cohort studies.

claim: PPARG is amplified in 17% of bladder cancer cases.
source: Copy number analysis identified PPARG as amplified in 17% of bladder cancer cases (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014), with PPARG amplified cases being highly enriched for PPARG mRNA expression (q value = 2.6 × 10-9) (Cerami et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to TCGA copy number analysis.

claim: PPARG amplified cases are highly enriched for PPARG mRNA expression (q value = 2.6 × 10-9).
source: Copy number analysis identified PPARG as amplified in 17% of bladder cancer cases (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014), with PPARG amplified cases being highly enriched for PPARG mRNA expression (q value = 2.6 × 10-9) (Cerami et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation and includes a specific statistical measure (q value).

claim: Hyperactive PPAR signaling may drive 20-25% of human bladder cancers.
source: These data raised the possibility that hyperactive PPAR signaling, either due to gene-amplification-driven hyper-expression or RXRA hot-spot mutation may drive 20–25% of bladder cancers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined frequency of PPARG amplification (17%) and RXRA mutations (5-8%).

claim: RXRA S427F mutation induces up-regulation of genes in the PPAR signaling pathway in JMSU-1 and 575A bladder cancer cell lines.
source: Gene transcripts robustly up-regulated by the mutation (twofold, FDR <0.05) were analyzed using over-representation analysis (ORA) to identify enriched pathways. In both cell lines, the PPAR signaling pathway (KEGG-hsa03320) was the top scoring hit.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing gene expression changes and pathway enrichment analysis, as shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Transcriptome changes induced by RXRA S427F mutation correlate with those induced by PPARG agonist pioglitazone treatment in JMSU-1 cells (Pearson r = 0.72, p=1.4 × 10−34).
source: There was robust correlation in both JMSU-1 and 575A (Pearson r = 0.72, p=1.4 × 10−34 or 3.1 × 10−105), confirming that the mutation drives expression changes similar to agonist-induced PPAR activation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical correlation analysis of RNA-seq data comparing mutation and agonist effects.

claim: Transcriptome changes induced by RXRA S427F mutation correlate with those induced by PPARG agonist pioglitazone treatment in 575A cells (Pearson r = 0.72, p=3.1 × 10−105).
source: There was robust correlation in both JMSU-1 and 575A (Pearson r = 0.72, p=1.4 × 10−34 or 3.1 × 10−105), confirming that the mutation drives expression changes similar to agonist-induced PPAR activation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical correlation analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: RXRA S427Y mutation also causes hyper-activation of PLIN2 and FABP3 in JMSU-1 cells.
source: Mutation-driven hyper-activation of PLIN2 and FABP3, two genes found up-regulated in our RNA-seq analysis, also occured in the context of RXRAS427Y in JMSU-1 cells (Figure 1D), confirming gain-of-function with either aromatic substitution.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: RXRA mutations cause up-regulation of PLIN2 expression in human bladder cancer specimens.
source: Previous analysis of human bladder cancer specimens identified a correlation between the presence of RXRAS427F/Y and both the up-regulation of PLIN2 expression and PPAR signaling pathway activity (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to TCGA analysis of clinical specimens.

claim: RXRA mutations cause increased PPAR signaling pathway activity in human bladder cancer specimens.
source: Previous analysis of human bladder cancer specimens identified a correlation between the presence of RXRAS427F/Y and both the up-regulation of PLIN2 expression and PPAR signaling pathway activity (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to TCGA analysis.

claim: Approximately 12% of RXRA-bound active enhancers/promoters show significant up-regulation in RXRA S427F mutant cells compared to wild-type (FDR <0.05).
source: ~12% of RAEs showed significant up-regulation in the mutant condition (FDR <0.05) (Figure 1E, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The canonical RXR/PPAR (DR1) motif is enriched at enhancers/promoters hyper-activated by mutant RXRA.
source: Consistent with activation of PPAR pathway genes, the canonical RXR/PPAR (DR1) motif was the only known motif found to be enriched with significant q-value.
evidence: This claim is supported by HOMER motif analysis of ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Mutant RXRA S427F shows hyper-activation of a DR1-driven luciferase reporter compared to wild-type RXRA in JMSU-1 cells.
source: Using transient transfection of a DR1-driven luciferase reporter, we confirmed relative hyper-activation of DR1 in the JMSU-1 cells expressing mutant RXRA compared to wild-type (Figure 1F), with a degree of induction similar to that observed after pioglitazone treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PPARG and PPARD are significantly more highly expressed than PPARA in bladder cancer specimens with mutant RXRA.
source: TCGA data were first queried to determine which of the three PPARs are most highly expressed in bladder cancer specimens with mutant RXRA (Cerami et al., 2012). Both PPARG and PPARD were significantly more highly expressed than PPARA, but the relative proportion of PPARG and PPARD varied amongst the samples (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of TCGA expression data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Combined knock-down of PPARD and PPARG strongly inhibits RXRA S427F-driven hyper-expression of PLIN2 and FABP3 in JMSU-1 and 575A cells.
source: Combined knock-down of PPARD and PPARG, however, strongly inhibited RXRAS427F-driven hyper-expression of both genes, to an extent greater than knockdown of PPARG alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Both PPARD and PPARG contribute to mutant RXRA-mediated transcriptional hyperactivity in human bladder cancer cells and have redundant function.
source: Thus, both PPARD and PPARG contribute to mutant RXRA-mediated transcriptional hyperactivity in human bladder cancer cells and appear to have redundant function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the siRNA knockdown experiments showing that both receptors are required for full activity.

claim: RXRA S427F/Y mutations do not confer gain-of-function in the RXRA homodimer context.
source: Since RXRA can drive transcription as a homodimer with a preference for the DR1 motif, these data indicate that the mutation does not confer gain-of-function in the homodimer context.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of hyperactivity in UM-UC-3 cells without PPAR co-transfection, as shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Expression of either PPARG or PPARD is sufficient to elicit mutant RXRA-associated hyperactivity in UM-UC-3 cells.
source: Expression of either PPAR was sufficient to elicit mutant RXRA associated hyperactivity to an extent that approximated agonist induced activation of the PPAR in the wild-type RXRA condition (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data with PPAR co-transfection shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mutant RXRA does not show increased activity with retinoic acid receptor alpha (RARA) compared to wild-type RXRA.
source: Both the DR1 reporter and a reporter with the preferred RXR/RAR binding motif, DR5, were induced by the RAR agonist all-trans-retinoic acid, but mutant RXRA did not elicit greater activity than wild-type RXRA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: RXRA hot-spot mutations confer gain-of-function selectively in the context of PPAR expression.
source: These data confirmed that RXRA hot-spot mutations confer gain-of-function selectively in the context of PPAR expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing activity with PPARs but not with RARA or in homodimer context.

claim: RXRA S427 resides in helix 10 at a heterodimerization interface in the RXRA/PPARG heterodimer.
source: Solved crystal structures of the RXRA/PPARG heterodimer reveal that RXRA S427 resides in helix 10 at a heterodimerization interface (Figure 3A) (Chandra et al., 2008; Gampe et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published crystal structures and visualization in Figure 3A.

claim: PPARG Q286P mutation completely blocks pioglitazone-driven receptor activation.
source: The Q286P mutation completely blocked pioglitazone-driven receptor activation, but RXRA S427F-driven receptor hyperactivity was maintained (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: RXRA S427F-driven receptor hyperactivity is maintained in PPARG Q286P mutant.
source: The Q286P mutation completely blocked pioglitazone-driven receptor activation, but RXRA S427F-driven receptor hyperactivity was maintained (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: PPARG E471A mutation strongly reduces both pioglitazone and RXRA S427F-driven activity.
source: In contrast, the PPARG E471A mutation previously characterized to diminish the transactivation activity of the PPARG AF2 (Chen et al., 2000), strongly reduced both pioglitazone and RXRA S427F-driven activity (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3B and citation to previous characterization.

claim: RXRA E453A mutation diminishes activation by the RXRA agonist SR11237 but has no impact on mutation-driven hyperactivity.
source: The analogous AF2 mutation in RXRA, E453A, diminished activation by the RXRA agonist SR11237, but had no impact on mutation-driven hyperactivity (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: RXRA S427F hyperactivity relies primarily on the PPAR AF2, independent of PPAR agonist binding.
source: These data support a model in which RXRAS427F hyperactivity relies primarily on the PPAR AF2, independent of PPAR agonist binding.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the mutational studies showing dependence on PPAR AF2 but not ligand binding pocket.

claim: Wild-type and mutant RXRA largely populate different conformational clusters in molecular dynamics simulations.
source: The wild-type and mutant largely populate different clusters, consistent with our hypothesis that mutant and wild-type RXRA differentially regulate the PPARG AF2 region (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This claim is supported by Markov State Model analysis of molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In RXRA S427F mutant simulations, PPARG E471 more closely approximates the agonist conformation.
source: In the RXRA mutant condition, PPARG E471 more closely approximated the agonist confirmation, in agreement with our mutational studies showing the importance of this residue.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of molecular dynamics simulation structures shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There is a significant difference in inter-residue distance between RXRA 427 and PPARG 477 in wild-type versus mutant RXRA simulations.
source: Comparing the 5% most frequently occupied clusters for wild type and mutant, we observed a significant difference in inter-residue distance between RXRA 427 and PPARG 477 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of molecular dynamics simulation data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Deletion or mutation to serine of the terminal tyrosine in PPARG (Y477) eliminates RXRA S427F-mediated hyperactivity while maintaining agonist inducibility.
source: In all cases, inducibility by agonist was maintained, but RXRA S427F-mediated hyperactivity was eliminated.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Deletion or mutation to serine of the terminal tyrosine in PPARD (Y441) eliminates RXRA S427F-mediated hyperactivity while maintaining agonist inducibility.
source: In all cases, inducibility by agonist was maintained, but RXRA S427F-mediated hyperactivity was eliminated.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: S427F/Y initiates an allosteric relay via an aromatic interaction with the terminal tyrosine on PPAR, leading to PPAR AF2 activation.
source: We conclude that S427F/Y initiates an allosteric relay via an aromatic interaction with the terminal tyrosine on PPAR, leading to PPAR AF2 activation.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion drawn from the combination of molecular dynamics simulations and mutational studies.

claim: No other RXR dimerization partners have an aromatic amino acid at the position corresponding to the terminal tyrosine in PPARs.
source: No other RXR dimerization partners have an aromatic amino acid at the corresponding position, providing a structural basis for the selective activation of PPARs (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Treatment of wild-type urothelial organoids with PPARD agonist GW0742 or PPARG agonist pioglitazone has no significant effect on growth in the absence of EGF.
source: Treatment with the PPARD agonist GW0742 or the PPARG agonist pioglitazone had no significant effect on growth in these conditions, suggesting that PPAR activation is not sufficient to drive growth in normal urothelial organoids (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by CellTiter-Glo growth assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: PPAR activation is not sufficient to drive growth in normal urothelial organoids.
source: Treatment with the PPARD agonist GW0742 or the PPARG agonist pioglitazone had no significant effect on growth in these conditions, suggesting that PPAR activation is not sufficient to drive growth in normal urothelial organoids (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the lack of growth response to PPAR agonists in wild-type organoids.

claim: Of 16 patient samples with RXRA hot-spot mutation, four had mutations in both TP53 and KDM6A, five had mutations in TP53 only, three had mutations in KDM6A only, and four had mutations in neither.
source: Of 16 patient samples identified with an RXRA hot-spot mutation across three cohorts, four had mutations in both TP53 and KDM6A, five had mutations in TP53 only, three had mutations in KDM6A only, and four had mutations in neither (Cerami et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of TCGA data cited.

claim: Elimination of Trp53 is sufficient for PPARD agonist GW0742 to drive proliferation of mouse urothelial organoids in EGF-depleted media.
source: Elimination of Trp53, but not Kdm6a, was sufficient for GW0742 to drive proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid growth assay data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Combined knock-out of Trp53 and Kdm6a results in more robust growth induction by GW0742 than Trp53 knock-out alone.
source: With combined knock-out of Trp53 and Kdm6a, growth induction by GW0742 was even more robust than with Trp53 knock-out alone.
evidence: This claim is supported by organoid growth assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Loss of tumor suppressors creates a context permissive for PPARD-driven proliferation.
source: These data suggest that loss of tumor suppressors creates a context permissive for PPARD-driven proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the differential growth responses to PPAR agonists in different genetic contexts.

claim: DKO 431.A organoids show strong, dose-dependent, enhanced growth when treated with GW0742 but not pioglitazone.
source: DKO 431.A showed strong, dose-dependent, enhanced growth when treated with GW0742, but not pioglitazone (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by CellTiter-Glo growth assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: GW0742 strongly induces expression of Plin2 and Fabp4 in DKO 431.A organoids, while pioglitazone has little to no effect.
source: GW0742 strongly induced both genes, while pioglitazone and little to no effect (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The ability of PPAR agonists to induce target genes in DKO 431.A correlates with their ability to promote growth-factor-independent growth.
source: These findings confirm that the ability of PPAR agonists to induce target genes in DKO 431.A correlates with their ability to promote growth-factor-independent growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing transcriptional and growth data.

claim: Mutant RXRA S427F-expressing organoids grow significantly faster than empty vector or wild-type RXRA-expressing organoids in EGF-depleted media.
source: Growth of the organoids in EGF deplete media was then assessed. Mutant RXRA-expressing organoids grew significantly faster than empty vector or wild-type expressing organoids (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by CellTiter-Glo growth assay data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Mutant RXRA S427F organoids show consistent growth over six passages while wild-type RXRA organoids plateau.
source: Mutant RXRA organoids showed consistent growth throughout the experiment, while the wild-type condition appeared to plateau (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by long-term organoid passaging and counting data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The difference in number of doublings per passage between mutant and wild-type RXRA organoids is highly significant (paired t test p=0.0003).
source: Comparing the number of doublings per passage between the two conditions, we found the difference to be highly significant (paired t test p=0.0003), confirming gain-of-function with the mutant allele.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of organoid growth data over multiple passages.

claim: Plin2 and Fabp4 are significantly up-regulated in mutant RXRA S427F organoids compared to empty vector or wild-type RXRA organoids.
source: Comparing vehicle-treated samples, Plin2 and Fabp4 were found significantly up-regulated in the mutant condition compared to the empty vector or wild-type organoids, confirming that mutant RXRA up-regulates expected PPAR targets in the organoid system (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Treatment of mutant RXRA-expressing organoids with PPARD inverse agonists ST247 and GSK0660 blunts up-regulation of Plin2 and Fabp4.
source: Treatment of the mutant expressing organoids with either of two PPARD inverse agonists, ST247 and GSK0660, blunted up-regulation of the target genes (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) (Naruhn et al., 2011; Shearer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PPARG antagonist T0070907 does not show inhibitory activity on PPAR target gene expression in mutant RXRA organoids.
source: The PPARG antagonist T0070907 did not show any inhibitory activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Mutant RXRA drives PPARD hyper-activity in the organoid system.
source: These findings confirm that mutant RXRA drives PPARD hyper-activity in the organoid system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene expression and antagonist studies in organoids.

claim: Mutant RXRA-expressing organoids show significant, dose-dependent growth inhibition when treated with PPARD antagonists ST247 or GSK0660.
source: When treated with either of the two PPARD antagonists, the mutant expressing organoids showed significant, dose-dependent growth inhibition (Figure 5B.)
evidence: This claim is supported by CellTiter-Glo growth assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Treatment of MCB6C organoids (carcinogen-induced bladder tumor line without RXRA mutation) with PPARD inhibitors does not inhibit growth in EGF-depleted media.
source: Treatment of MCB6C with the PPARD inhibitors in EGF deplete media did not inhibit their growth across the identical doses (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by CellTiter-Glo growth assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PPARG antagonist T0070907 has no antiproliferative effects on mutant RXRA-expressing organoids.
source: As expected based on the gene expression analysis, the PPARG antagonist T0070907 also had no antiproliferative effects on 431.A.RXRAS427F (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by CellTiter-Glo growth assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: PPAR antagonists do not significantly inhibit growth of wild-type RXRA organoids in EGF-containing media.
source: Lastly, 431.A.RXRwt organoids in EGF-containing media were treated with the same PPAR antagonists, none of which significantly inhibited growth of this organoid line (Figure 5E), confirming PPAR dependence is specific to mutant RXRA-driven proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by CellTiter-Glo growth assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PPAR dependence is specific to mutant RXRA-driven proliferation.
source: Lastly, 431.A.RXRwt organoids in EGF-containing media were treated with the same PPAR antagonists, none of which significantly inhibited growth of this organoid line (Figure 5E), confirming PPAR dependence is specific to mutant RXRA-driven proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing PPAR antagonist effects in different genetic and growth contexts.

claim: A role for PPAR activity in promoting bladder cancer is supported by the presence of PPARG gene amplification in 17% of cases.
source: A role for PPAR activity in promoting bladder cancer is supported by the presence of a PPARG gene amplification in 17% of cases (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to TCGA copy number data.

claim: Pioglitazone use in patients with diabetes appears to increase bladder cancer risk.
source: Intriguingly, pioglitazone use in patients with diabetes appears to increase bladder cancer risk, further hinting that PPARG activation can promote bladder cancer growth (Lewis et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to an epidemiological study.

claim: Human bladder cancer samples express both PPARD and PPARG.
source: Importantly, human bladder cancer samples appear to express both PPARD and PPARG and our data suggest both are activated by mutant RXRA and play a role in transcriptional hyperactivity in human bladder cancer cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA expression data shown in Figure 2A,B and functional studies.

claim: Both PPARD and PPARG are activated by mutant RXRA and play a role in transcriptional hyperactivity in human bladder cancer cells.
source: Importantly, human bladder cancer samples appear to express both PPARD and PPARG and our data suggest both are activated by mutant RXRA and play a role in transcriptional hyperactivity in human bladder cancer cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by siRNA knockdown experiments and reporter assays showing both receptors contribute to mutant RXRA activity.

claim: RXR agonists can induce activation of RXR/PPAR heterodimers independent of the RXR AF2 by inducing conformational changes in PPAR.
source: Heyman and colleagues showed two decades ago that RXR agonists can induce activation of RXR/PPAR heterodimers, independent of the RXR AF2, by inducing conformational changes in PPAR (Schulman et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by Heyman and colleagues.

claim: PPAR activation is only sufficient to drive growth of urothelial organoids with concurrent tumor suppressor loss.
source: In contrast to classical growth factors such as EGF which stimulate proliferation of wild-type organoids, we found that PPARD activation is only sufficient to drive growth with concurrent tumor suppressor loss.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing growth responses in wild-type versus tumor suppressor knockout organoids.

claim: Bladder cancer is the sixth most common cancer in the US.
source: Bladder cancer is the sixth most common cancer in the US and is predicted to cause ~17,000 deaths in 2017 [The website of the National Cancer Institute (https://www.cancer.gov)].
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to National Cancer Institute statistics.

claim: Bladder cancer is predicted to cause approximately 17,000 deaths in 2017.
source: Bladder cancer is the sixth most common cancer in the US and is predicted to cause ~17,000 deaths in 2017 [The website of the National Cancer Institute (https://www.cancer.gov)].
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to National Cancer Institute predictions.

claim: Bladder cancer management has not yet benefited from molecularly targeted therapies.
source: In contrast to other common malignancies, bladder cancer management has not yet benefited from molecularly targeted therapies.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of bladder cancer treatment based on established knowledge.

claim: Early phase clinical data with agents targeting FGFR3 or ERBB family members have shown encouraging activity in the minority of patients with oncogenic versions of these kinases.
source: Early phase clinical data with agents targeting FGFR3 or ERBB family members have shown encouraging activity in the minority of patients with oncogenic versions of these kinases (Nogova et al., 2017; Choudhury et al., 2016), but identification of new targetable genomic drivers is needed to expand the armamentarium.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical trial data.

claim: Nuclear receptors are amongst the most successful therapeutic targets in oncology.
source: Nuclear receptors are amongst the most successful therapeutic targets in oncology, with small molecule inhibitors of estrogen receptor (ER) and androgen receptor (AR) improving survival in breast and prostate cancers (Fisher et al., 1996; Beer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies showing survival benefit.

claim: Small molecule inhibitors of estrogen receptor and androgen receptor improve survival in breast and prostate cancers.
source: Nuclear receptors are amongst the most successful therapeutic targets in oncology, with small molecule inhibitors of estrogen receptor (ER) and androgen receptor (AR) improving survival in breast and prostate cancers (Fisher et al., 1996; Beer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: TP53 is mutated in approximately 50% of bladder cancer cases.
source: For our analysis, we focused on TP53 and KDM6A which are amongst the most frequently mutated tumor suppressors in bladder cancer, mutated in ~50% and~25% of bladder cancer cases, respectively (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Guo et al., 2013; Van Allen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three independent cohort studies.

claim: KDM6A is mutated in approximately 25% of bladder cancer cases.
source: For our analysis, we focused on TP53 and KDM6A which are amongst the most frequently mutated tumor suppressors in bladder cancer, mutated in ~50% and~25% of bladder cancer cases, respectively (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Guo et al., 2013; Van Allen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three independent cohort studies.
